strengths: The paper tackles an important problem for VLA-based autonomous driving: moving beyond sparse trajectory/text supervision and pure behavior cloning. The combination of future RGB/depth generation with trajectory prediction is well motivated and fits current world-model directions in autonomous driving.

The experimental results on NAVSIM are strong. The method reports 93.7 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with best-of-N and 88.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, including competitive or best sub-metrics, despite using only a single front camera.
Ablations support the value of dense visual supervision: RGB and depth generation each improve the Stage 1 model, and their combination gives a clear gain over trajectory-only training.
The paper is generally clear, with a readable architecture/training description, relevant related work, and useful qualitative visualizations for planning and generated future RGB/depth outputs.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim, uncertainty-based exploration, is not strongly validated. The reward ablation shows only a very small gain from adding the image reward over PDMS-only RL on NAVSIM v1, from 90.19 to 90.36 PDMS, so most of the Stage 2 improvement appears to come from optimizing PDMS directly rather than the proposed exploration signal.

The paper treats world-model prediction entropy as a novelty measure, but the connection is asserted more than demonstrated. Entropy can reflect ambiguous or hard-to-predict visual futures, model miscalibration, or image-token uncertainty unrelated to useful trajectory novelty. The analysis in Fig. 3 is qualitative and lacks quantitative calibration, correlation statistics, or comparisons to simpler novelty measures.

The RL/exploration setup is underspecified for a safety-critical autonomous-driving claim. NAVSIM is non-reactive, and it is unclear how sampled candidate trajectories interact with the world model and PDMS evaluation during training, how stable GRPO is, and whether the learned policy truly explores useful alternatives rather than exploiting benchmark-specific reward structure.

The strongest headline NAVSIM v1 result uses a best-of-N strategy. Without best-of-N, ExploreVLA reaches 90.4 PDMS, which is not state of the art compared with several listed methods; the paper should more carefully separate single-sample policy quality from reranking/sampling benefits.

Generalization evidence is limited. On nuScenes, only Stage 1 is evaluated and the method is not clearly superior: its ST-P3 average L2 is worse than several baselines, and UniAD-protocol collision results are absent. This weakens claims that the exploration mechanism improves out-of-distribution or cross-benchmark robustness.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives useful hyperparameters, but important details such as model scale, exact prompt/output formatting, image-token masking scheme, reward normalization function f, GRPO implementation specifics, and full training/evaluation code availability are not sufficiently specified in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: improving VLA-based autonomous driving beyond behavior cloning by adding dense world-model supervision and post-training with a safety-aware reward.

The unified prediction of trajectories, future RGB, and future depth is a plausible and relevant design choice. The Stage-1 ablations suggest that RGB and depth generation improve NAVSIM v1 PDMS over a trajectory-only baseline.
The reported NAVSIM v2 result is strong, with ExploreVLA achieving the best EPDMS among the listed methods, and the paper includes comparisons across several recent driving planners.

The method is reasonably easy to follow at a high level, and the supplement provides some useful implementation details such as backbone, input resolution, depth source, GRPO group size, LoRA rank, and training schedule.
weaknesses: The central claim about novelty-aware exploration is weakly supported. The image-reward contribution over PDMS-only GRPO is extremely small in Table 4: PDMS improves from 90.19 to 90.36, while image reward alone is essentially ineffective. This does not convincingly establish that world-model uncertainty drives meaningful exploration beyond the task reward.

The uncertainty formulation is underspecified and potentially flawed. Eq. 5 appears to use the probability of generated tokens rather than the entropy over each token's full codebook distribution, and the normalization function f is not defined. There is no calibration analysis showing that this uncertainty reliably measures OOD behavior rather than image-generation ambiguity, occlusion, or scene complexity.

The RL setup is not convincingly described for autonomous driving. The paper discusses exploration and trial-and-error, but NAVSIM is non-reactive/offline, and it is unclear how sampled continuous trajectories condition the future image generator, how rewards are computed during training, and whether this is truly exploration or simply reward-based reranking/fine-tuning on benchmark metrics.

The empirical case relies heavily on NAVSIM benchmark scores, while the claimed generalization is not strongly demonstrated. On nuScenes, ExploreVLA is not state of the art in L2 error, lacks UniAD collision results, and Stage 2 is not evaluated, which weakens the evidence that the proposed exploration mechanism generalizes.

The comparisons are somewhat hard to interpret. The headline NAVSIM v1 result uses a best-of-N strategy, while the non-best-of-N model is below several recent methods; the paper does not sufficiently discuss the computational or deployment implications of best-of-N sampling.

Important reproducibility details are missing or vague, including exact model scale, prompts/instructions, masking strategy, reward normalization, GRPO objective details, action sampling temperature, training data volume, and the promised code link is blank in the abstract.

Several claims are overstated relative to evidence. For example, the paper asserts discovery of novel successful strategies, but provides only a small qualitative visualization and a coarse correlation plot, without measuring behavioral diversity, safety under distribution shift, uncertainty calibration, or closed-loop robustness.

The limitations section is too narrow. It mentions only single front-view input and possible BEV targets, but does not address more serious concerns such as monocular-depth pseudo-label noise, offline reward bias, uncertainty miscalibration, non-reactive simulation limitations, and safety implications of encouraging high-uncertainty trajectories.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: improving VLA-based end-to-end driving beyond pure behavior cloning by combining dense world modeling with RL-style post-training. The framing is well motivated for autonomous driving, where sparse waypoint/text supervision is plausibly insufficient.

The method is technically coherent: a unified Show-o-style backbone jointly predicts trajectories and future RGB/depth tokens, and the world model uncertainty is used as an intrinsic exploration bonus gated by PDMS. The training recipe and main hyperparameters are described in enough detail to make the approach broadly reproducible.

Empirical results on NAVSIM are strong. The method reports state-of-the-art PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with best-of-N sampling and the best EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, including competitive or best performance on many safety/compliance submetrics while using only a single front-view camera.

The ablations support the dense supervision component convincingly: adding RGB or depth generation improves over trajectory-only training, and combining both yields the best Stage-1 PDMS. This is a meaningful contribution even independent of the exploration reward.

The paper includes useful qualitative evidence for both improved planning after RL post-training and future RGB/depth generation quality. The limitations section is concise and acknowledges single-view sensing and possible additional scene-structure targets.
weaknesses: The central exploration-reward claim is less strongly supported than the dense-supervision claim. In Table 4, adding the image-based exploration reward on top of PDMS reward improves PDMS only from 90.19 to 90.36, a small gain that may be within run-to-run variance; no statistical analysis or repeated seeds are reported.

The uncertainty-as-novelty mechanism is asserted more than rigorously validated. Figure 3 gives a limited qualitative/correlation analysis, but the paper does not show whether high entropy reliably corresponds to useful OOD but safe behaviors across scenarios, nor does it compare against simpler novelty measures or uncertainty estimators.

The RL setting is somewhat under-specified conceptually. The method relies on NAVSIM/PDMS scoring of sampled trajectories rather than true interactive environment rollouts, so the extent to which this constitutes meaningful exploration of state transitions is debatable. This matters because exploration beyond demonstrations is one of the main claimed contributions.

Some comparisons could be clarified for fairness. The strongest NAVSIM v1 number uses best-of-N sampling, while the non-best-of-N result is below several leaderboard methods; computational cost and inference-time implications of best-of-N are not discussed. Multi-view/LiDAR comparisons are interesting but not strictly apples-to-apples.

The nuScenes generalization evidence is mixed. ExploreVLA has competitive collision rates, but its L2 errors are worse than several VLA baselines under ST-P3 and UniAD protocols, and Stage-2 RL is not evaluated there. This limits the strength of the generalization claim.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete: the code is promised rather than available in the manuscript, and details such as exact reward normalization function f, image-token entropy computation, model size/training cost, and variance across runs would be important for reproducing and interpreting the gains.
